strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: group-wise training-data attribution for diffusion models, with a clear counterfactual framing and practical motivation such as copyright assessment and fair compensation.

Proposes a novel and efficient idea: approximating expensive Leave-One-Group-Out retraining with machine unlearning, and instantiates it for both unconditional (Guda-U) and conditional text-to-image (Guda-C) settings.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and UnlearnCanvas include multiple ranking metrics, hyperparameter ablations, qualitative examples, and wall-clock timing, showing promising head-identification gains over CLIPA and Wang et al. on the conditional task.
The paper is generally well organized, with a helpful overview figure (Fig. 1) and an extensive appendix that details model architectures, training configurations, and evaluation protocols.
The impact statement acknowledges that unlearning is used as a computational approximation rather than certified deletion, and discusses broader ethical implications.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for Guda-U in Appendix A.1 is flawed. It claims Eq. (15) is an unbiased reformulation of the retain-only objective L_ret. However, changing the sampling distribution of x_t from p_ret,t to p_for,t without the importance weight p_ret,t/p_for,t yields a different objective. Thus Eq. (15) does not equal L_ret up to a variance term, and the claim that ReTrack targets the same LOGO counterfactual is unsupported.

The LOGO oracle used for evaluation is not a true counterfactual. On CIFAR-10, the full model excludes one random class per epoch, so it never sees the full dataset in any epoch, deviating from a standard full-data model. On UnlearnCanvas, LOGO models are fine-tuned from the same pretrained SD 1.5 checkpoint rather than retrained from scratch, so they are practical proxies, not true leave-one-group-out models.

All attribution metrics are computed against LOGOA, which is itself an ELBO-difference score between the full and LOGO models. There is no external ground truth (e.g., the known class or style used to generate an image) to validate that LOGOA identifies true causal influence. GUDA is therefore evaluated mainly on how well it approximates another ELBO-based score, making the central attribution claim circular.

The computational cost comparison is inconsistent and overstates the speedup. The text states that LOGOA requires training N+1 models while GUDA trains the full model once plus N unlearning runs. However, Table 1 reports GUDA preprocessing of only 1:07, which appears to exclude full-model training, whereas LOGOA preprocessing of 206:52 includes it. If full-model training were included for both, the CIFAR-10 speedup would be roughly 10x, not the claimed 100x.

On CIFAR-10, GUDA is essentially tied with DAS on the main metrics (72.7% vs 71.6% Top-1; 0.677 vs 0.675 NDCG@3), yet the paper repeatedly claims that GUDA substantially outperforms gradient-based attribution. The true advantage over DAS is computational, not accuracy. On UnlearnCanvas, the absolute Top-1 is only 45.6%, meaning more than half of top-1 predictions disagree with the proxy oracle, limiting practical usefulness.

The UnlearnCanvas evaluation is restricted to 16 alphabetically selected styles out of 60 training styles. This arbitrary subset may not be representative, and the true most influential style could lie among the 44 unevaluated styles. Both predictions and ground truth are limited to this subset, so the reported ranking is incomplete.

The conditional method Guda-C is largely heuristic. The anchor-redirection objective is not derived from the LOGO counterfactual; the paper acknowledges that a naive conditional extension of ReTrack fails but does not provide a principled replacement. There is no ablation on anchor construction or comparison to other conditional unlearning methods such as ESD or Forget-Me-Not.

ELBO is used as a scoring rule without empirical validation that it preserves likelihood ordering or correlates with true attribution. The paper acknowledges that ELBO is only a lower bound but provides no check of its reliability. No uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, so small metric differences may not be meaningful.

The baseline set is limited. Despite discussing group-level Shapley methods (Data Shapley, CS-Shapley) and other group influence approaches in related work, the experiments do not compare against them. On UnlearnCanvas, only CLIPA and Wang et al. are compared, with no gradient-based or group-level influence baselines.

Reproducibility is incomplete: full descriptor vocabularies, exact evaluation prompts, and code are not provided. The descriptor extraction with Qwen2.5-VL is not fully specified, and the inconsistent cost accounting makes the reported efficiency claims difficult to reproduce or verify.

The paper contains several overclaims, including 'substantially outperforms' for marginal CIFAR-10 gains and '~100x speedup' that is likely inflated by inconsistent accounting. Such claims reduce trust in the empirical conclusions.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: group-wise training data attribution for diffusion models, with applications in copyright assessment, fair compensation, and model debugging.
Proposes a conceptually appealing framework (GUDA) that uses machine unlearning to approximate expensive Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) retraining, enabling scalable counterfactual attribution.
Includes a LOGO oracle for evaluation, which provides a ground-truth counterfactual for comparison and is a strong methodological choice.
Reports significant computational speedups over LOGO retraining (e.g., ~100x on CIFAR-10) and provides detailed wall-clock timing breakdowns.
Conducts ablation studies (e.g., effect of unlearning epochs, K-NN, learning rate) that offer some insight into the method's behavior.
Includes an impact statement that acknowledges limitations and potential risks, demonstrating awareness of ethical considerations.
weaknesses: The core claim that unlearning approximates the LOGO counterfactual is not rigorously validated. The theoretical justification in Appendix A.1 is only for the unconditional case and relies on an idealized equivalence that is subsequently approximated (K-NN truncation, finite steps, preservation term). The paper does not quantify the approximation error or provide any bounds.

Empirical validation shows only moderate agreement with the LOGOA oracle: 72.7% top-1 on CIFAR-10 and 45.6% top-1 on UnlearnCanvas. On UnlearnCanvas, GUDA fails to identify the top group more than half the time, which raises doubts about the practical utility of the attribution.

Baselines are not strong or fairly tuned. TRAK performs near random (11.8% top-1 on CIFAR-10), suggesting possible implementation issues rather than a fundamental limitation. The Wang et al. (2024) baseline, an instance-level method adapted to group attribution, also performs near random (4.7% top-1), which may not be a fair comparison.

No comparison against a strong group-level attribution baseline (e.g., group influence functions or Shapley-based methods). The only baselines are semantic similarity and instance-level methods, which are not directly designed for group-wise attribution.

The conditional unlearning method (Guda-C) is heuristic and lacks theoretical grounding. The anchor construction via CLIP-weighted style selection is ad-hoc and not justified theoretically, unlike the unconditional ReTrack-based approach.

Evaluation is limited in scale: CIFAR-10 is described as 'preliminary' and 'proof of concept', and UnlearnCanvas attribution is only computed for 16 out of 60 styles, restricting the practical significance.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or models are released, and some hyperparameters (e.g., number of steps per epoch for CIFAR-10 unlearning) are not fully specified. The 'exposure-matched training' details are unclear.
Presentation issues: inconsistent notation (e.g., 'Guda' vs 'GUDA', a typo 'θ^{rel}_{-k}' in Algorithm 1), and dense sections that are hard to follow, particularly the conditional unlearning details.
The paper dismisses Spearman correlation as less important, but the reported values (e.g., 0.239 on UnlearnCanvas) indicate poor full-ranking agreement, which is relevant for attribution quality.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: group-wise counterfactual attribution for diffusion models, with clear applications to copyright assessment, fair compensation, and model debugging.

Introduces a novel and intuitive framing: using machine unlearning to approximate Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) counterfactual models, avoiding the prohibitive cost of retraining N+1 models from scratch.

Provides two concrete instantiations: unconditional generation via ReTrack-based redirection and conditional text-to-image attribution via weighted style-selection anchors, with detailed algorithmic descriptions.
Reports meaningful computational savings: approximately 100x speedup over LOGO retraining on CIFAR-10 and 5.2x on UnlearnCanvas, with query-time costs comparable to the oracle and faster than DAS.
Shows promising empirical results on UnlearnCanvas, where GUDA outperforms CLIPA and the Wang et al. baseline on head-focused metrics such as Top-1, MRR, NDCG@3, and RBO.
Includes a substantial appendix with hyperparameters, ablation studies, prompt design, and evaluation metric definitions, reflecting a strong effort toward reproducibility.
Contains an honest impact statement discussing societal benefits, potential risks, and limitations.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification in Appendix A.1 is flawed: Eq. (15) is not an unbiased reformulation of the retain-only objective because x_t is sampled from the forget distribution p_for,t without any importance-weight correction. Therefore, the claim that ReTrack's untruncated objective equals the LOGO counterfactual training objective is incorrect, undermining a central theoretical motivation for the method.

The evaluation does not directly validate that the unlearned models approximate the LOGO counterfactual models. There is no comparison of θ^ul vs. θ^logo (e.g., parameter distance, generation similarity, or unlearning efficacy metrics); the paper only measures ranking agreement with LOGOA, which is an indirect and potentially insufficient validation of the approximation quality.

On CIFAR-10, GUDA's advantage over DAS is marginal and likely within noise: Top-1 72.7% vs. 71.6%, NDCG@3 0.677 vs. 0.675, and DAS actually has higher Spearman correlation (0.267 vs. 0.265). The paper's claim of 'substantially outperforming all baselines' is overstated, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

The main text-to-image experiment (UnlearnCanvas) lacks comparisons to strong gradient-based attribution baselines such as DAS or D-TRAK, which were competitive on CIFAR-10. It only compares against CLIPA and a potentially under-tuned Wang et al. baseline, leaving the practical advantage of GUDA for conditional attribution insufficiently established.

Directly relevant group-attribution baselines from the literature (e.g., group influence functions, Data Shapley, CS-Shapley) are discussed in related work but not evaluated empirically, despite the paper's motivation that instance-level aggregation fails due to nonlinear group interactions.

The conditional Guda-C method is heuristic: anchor redirection is not derived from a counterfactual objective, and there is no validation that the anchor prompts are on-distribution or that the unlearned model actually forgets the target style while preserving the retain set.

The ELBO-based scoring rule is not validated against log-likelihood or alternative scores. The paper acknowledges that ELBO may not preserve likelihood ordering, but provides no empirical check that ELBO differences reliably reflect counterfactual influence.

Reproducibility and robustness are limited by the absence of multiple random seeds or error bars, especially given the small query set (320) in the UnlearnCanvas experiment. The 'LOGO oracle' for UnlearnCanvas is itself a fine-tuning proxy rather than true retraining, which may bias the evaluation.

Several claims are overstated or inconsistent: for example, 'validated against LOGO' is stronger than what the indirect ranking metrics support; θ^rel is used but undefined; λ_prex is a typo; and the loss-weighting conventions differ substantially between CIFAR-10 and UnlearnCanvas despite the claim of mathematical equivalence by reparameterization.

strengths: Formalizes group-wise attribution as a counterfactual Leave-One-Group-Out (LOGO) estimand (LOGOA) and provides a clear likelihood-based scoring rule for diffusion models.

Proposes GUDA, an efficient framework that approximates LOGO counterfactual models via machine unlearning, with two instantiations for unconditional generation (ReTrack-based redirection) and conditional text-to-image style attribution (weighted style-selection anchors).
Validates against LOGO oracles on CIFAR-10 and UnlearnCanvas, comparing to semantic similarity (CLIPA), gradient-based attribution (DAS, D-TRAK, TRAK), and instance-level unlearning (Wang et al.).
Provides extensive ablations on the unlearning operator, K-nearest neighbors, loss weights, anchor strategies, and robustness to noisy group partitions, plus detailed timing analyses.
Reports a ~100x wall-clock speedup over LOGO retraining on CIFAR-10 and faster query-time evaluation than the gradient-based DAS baseline.
Includes a PF-ODE likelihood oracle validation on CIFAR-10 showing strong correlation between ΔELBO and Δlog p, supporting the use of ELBO as a practical surrogate.
Contains an honest limitations discussion and impact statement, including the caveat that the unlearning operator is not a certified deletion mechanism.
weaknesses: The evaluation is entirely relative to a LOGOA oracle that is not validated against known semantic ground truth. For UnlearnCanvas, the prompt style is known, yet the paper does not check whether LOGOA or GUDA top-1 matches that style; for CIFAR-10, generated samples have no known class label. This leaves the practical meaningfulness of the attribution target unverified.

The unlearning approximation is only validated indirectly via downstream attribution rankings. There is no direct comparison between the unlearned model θ_ul and the LOGO model θ_logo (e.g., output distribution distances, likelihood on retain/forget sets, or parameter distances), so the central claim that unlearning approximates the counterfactual model is not fully established.

Scalability is a core motivation, but experiments only use N=10 groups (CIFAR-10) and N=16 groups (UnlearnCanvas). Preprocessing and query-time both scale linearly with N, and storing N unlearned models is memory-intensive. The paper does not test larger N or discuss these scaling bottlenecks, so the 'practical at scale' claim is not well supported.

On CIFAR-10, GUDA's improvement over the DAS baseline is marginal (e.g., Top-1 0.727 vs. 0.716, NDCG@3 0.677 vs. 0.675), and under the PF-ODE likelihood oracle DAS is better on several metrics (NDCG@3, Top-3, Spearman). No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are provided, so the claim that GUDA reliably outperforms gradient-based attribution is overstated.

The conditional GUDA-C method lacks theoretical grounding analogous to the ReTrack derivation; it is a heuristic anchor-redirection scheme. It is only compared to CLIPA and a near-random Wang et al. baseline, with no comparison to other conditional unlearning operators (e.g., ESD, Forget-Me-Not) within the GUDA framework.

Several baseline implementations appear weak or untuned (TRAK near random at 11.8% Top-1; Wang et al. 4.7% Top-1), and the paper does not investigate whether these failures stem from implementation or aggregation choices rather than fundamental limitations, weakening the comparative conclusions.

Presentation issues: many bibliography year mismatches (e.g., Chen et al. cited as 2023 but listed 2025; Koh & Liang cited as 2023 but listed 2017), and the code URL is missing from the provided manuscript, hindering reproducibility.
No multiple-seed runs or error bars for the main results, making small differences between methods difficult to interpret.

strengths: Useful conceptual framing: formalizing group-wise attribution as a LOGO counterfactual estimand and proposing unlearning as a computational approximation is a sensible and clearly articulated idea (Sec. 3.3, Sec. 4).

The framework is instantiated in two settings (unconditional via ReTrack-style redirection, conditional via CLIP-weighted style anchors), with a shared preservation term, and the conditional anchor design (keep content, swap style) is a reasonable response to the prompt-distribution shift problem (Sec. 4.2.2, Appendix B.1).

The paper is generally well-written, with detailed hyperparameters, algorithmic description (Algorithm 1), and reproducibility information in the appendix (model configs, prompt construction, ELBO protocol).

Honest limitations discussion: the authors explicitly flag the ELBO surrogate, the unlearning approximation bias, the disjoint-partition assumption, and non-additivity (Appendix E), and they provide an ELBO-vs-likelihood validation study (Appendix D.5) rather than hiding the issue.
Reasonable evaluation design with multiple head-focused metrics (Top-1, MRR, NDCG@3, RBO) and a cost analysis separating preprocessing from query time (Sec. 4.3, Appendix D.3-D.4).
weaknesses: The central quantitative claim is overstated relative to the evidence. On CIFAR-10, GUDA (Top-1 0.727, NDCG@3 0.677) is essentially tied with DAS (0.716, 0.675); the abstract's claim that it identifies contributing groups 'more reliably than... gradient-based attribution' is not supported by a ~1-point gap, and no statistical significance or variance over seeds is reported.

The advantage is not robust under the stricter likelihood oracle the authors themselves construct. In Appendix D.5 Table 13(b), DAS matches or exceeds GUDA on NDCG@3 (0.630 vs 0.618), Top-3 (0.459 vs 0.435), and Spearman (0.236 vs 0.187). This directly undermines the paper's core argument that targeting the group-removal counterfactual is more effective than gradient-based attribution.

Low absolute accuracy on the more realistic setting: 45.6% Top-1 on UnlearnCanvas means GUDA fails to identify the primary style in more than half of queries, which limits the practical claims about copyright/fair-compensation use cases.

Limited novelty in the method itself: the unlearning operators (ReTrack, ESD) are existing methods and the scoring rule (ELBO difference) is standard; the contribution reduces largely to combining existing components, which the authors acknowledge ('the contribution is the LOGOA estimand..., not a novel unlearning algorithm', Sec. 2.3).

Potential circularity: both GUDA and the LOGOA oracle use the identical ELBO-difference scoring rule, so agreement between them is partly built into the construction; the comparison largely tests whether unlearning mimics retraining under a shared metric rather than whether either captures true group influence.

The 'oracle' is a proxy, not true LOGO: counterfactual models are obtained by fine-tuning from a shared SD 1.5 checkpoint with matched budgets (Sec. 5.2.1, Appendix C.2.2), not by training on D\D_k as defined in Sec. 3.3. This weakens the gold standard against which all methods are judged.

Baselines are not designed for the group-removal counterfactual (instance-level DAS/TRAK/D-TRAK, semantic similarity CLIPA), so outperforming them is a weak test of the central hypothesis; a group-aware second-order/Shapley-style baseline is absent from the comparisons.

Scalability is asserted but not demonstrated: experiments use only 10 and 16 groups, while the method requires one unlearning run per group (linear in N). The '~100x speedup' derives from unlearning using ~1/120 of the optimization steps, which may reflect a much weaker approximation rather than genuine efficiency of an equivalent operation, and query-time is identical to LOGO.

Odd, unjustified evaluation subset on UnlearnCanvas: attribution is restricted to 'the first 16 styles in alphabetical order' (Sec. 5.2.1) with no rationale or sensitivity check, and the CIFAR-10 vs UnlearnCanvas baselines differ (no DAS/TRAK on the conditional setting), preventing a consistent picture of where GUDA's advantage actually holds.

The reported Spearman correlations are very low across all methods (0.03-0.27), and the paper leans on head metrics partly to avoid this; while this is defensible, it also signals that no method, including GUDA, tracks the full counterfactual ranking well.

strengths: Formalizes group-wise counterfactual attribution for diffusion models around an explicit LOGOA estimand, using leave-one-group-out retraining as the oracle rather than relying only on semantic similarity or instance-level aggregation.

Proposes a practical framework that approximates expensive LOGO counterfactual models via machine unlearning from a shared full-data model, with precomputed per-group unlearned models that can be reused across queries.

Provides two instantiations: a theoretically motivated ReTrack-based unconditional redirection method and a conditional text-to-image extension using CLIP-weighted style-selection anchors to address prompt-distribution shift.
Includes a reasonably broad empirical evaluation on CIFAR-10 with true LOGO models and on UnlearnCanvas with Stable Diffusion 1.5, comparing against CLIPA, DAS, D-TRAK, TRAK, ESD, and Wang et al.

Reports substantial computational advantages in some settings, e.g., ~100x speedup over LOGO on CIFAR-10 and ~5.2x over LOGO plus ~17.8x over Wang et al. on UnlearnCanvas, with query-time amortization.
Contains useful ablations on unlearning epochs, forget-loss weight, K-nearest neighbors, learning rate, anchor strategy, DAS ridge regularization/aggregation, and noisy group partitions.
Validates the ELBO proxy against a PF-ODE likelihood oracle on CIFAR-10 (Pearson 0.820, Spearman 0.735, Top-1 agreement 0.683) and is transparent about the proxy's limitations.

Reproducibility is supported by detailed appendices covering architectures, hyperparameters, prompt construction, evaluation metrics, and an explicit limitations discussion plus an ethics/impact statement.
weaknesses: The central approximation has no formal guarantee: the practical Guda-U loss omits the density-ratio correction and truncates the importance-weighted sum to K nearest neighbors, so its fidelity to the LOGO counterfactual is established only empirically on limited benchmarks.

The text-to-image LOGO oracle is not a true leave-one-group-out retraining oracle: UnlearnCanvas LOGO models are fine-tuned from the same SD 1.5 checkpoint, so the estimand concerns removal from fine-tuning data rather than removal from all training data, weakening the counterfactual claim.

The attribution estimand relies on ELBO differences as a surrogate for log-likelihood differences; ELBO does not generally preserve likelihood ordering, and the PF-ODE validation is only on CIFAR-10 and itself approximate. Full-ranking correlations remain low (e.g., Spearman <0.27).

On CIFAR-10, the gains over the strongest gradient baseline DAS are marginal (Top-1 0.727 vs. 0.716; NDCG@3 0.677 vs. 0.675), and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the main tables, making small differences hard to interpret.

The conditional Guda-C anchor construction is heuristic rather than derived from a conditional LOGO objective. Training the unlearned model to match the frozen full model under CLIP-weighted retain-style anchors may partly encode prompt-style associations instead of isolating data influence.

Evaluation scope is limited: CIFAR-10 and only 16 of 60 UnlearnCanvas styles with 320 queries; there is no large-scale real-artist or LAION-style attribution experiment, and no DAS/TRAK-style gradient baseline is evaluated in the conditional setting.

Some baselines may be disadvantaged by adaptation choices: Wang et al. (2024) is an instance-level unlearning method adapted to group attribution and performs near-randomly, while TRAK is also near-random, so the comparison may not fully reflect the strongest possible group-level alternatives.

The method assumes a clean disjoint group partition. Robustness is tested only with 5% random reassignment on CIFAR-10; overlapping, hierarchical, or semantically ambiguous groups are not addressed, and non-additivity of group effects is left as future work.

The abstract says the code is available but the URL appears truncated/missing, and the computational requirements for Stable Diffusion fine-tuning and unlearning are substantial, which may limit exact reproduction by others.
